turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was more than one option, I think, near the middle of the screen, and I wasn't quite sure which one was the main one. Something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The two buttons at the bottom of the screen — "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" — are stacked in a sequence where the secondary action ("Continue Shopping") appears larger and more prominent above the primary action ("Place Order"), reversing the expected hierarchy.

B) The "Place Order" and "Continue Shopping" buttons are not grouped under any label or section heading, so there is no visual indication of what category of action they belong to or how they relate to the payment form above them.

C) The two item prices in the Order Summary are presented inconsistently — one ("$39.99") appears in a noticeably larger and bolder format than the other ("$249.00") — making it unclear whether one carries more significance than the other.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to).

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: If I had to pick... probably A? I think. Though I'm not sure that's exactly it — it might be closer to another option, depending on how you're defining it. It's more of a general feeling than a specific thing. Other people might not even notice.

turns.q: Looking at those two buttons at the bottom of the layout, what does the size and visual weight of "Continue Shopping" compared to "Place Order" suggest to you about which action this screen is designed around?
turns.a: There were two buttons near each other, I think. One of them seemed more... present than the other — like it had more weight to it. I kept looking at the more prominent one wondering if that was the main one. Or maybe the other one. I'm not really sure.

turns.q: If someone arrived at this layout having just filled in their payment details, would the uncertainty you're describing cause them to pause once and move on — or would it keep pulling their attention back to those two buttons?
turns.a: My eye kept going back to 'Continue Shopping' — scanning it as if it might be the confirmation step. Then I'd re-read both labels. I had to do that a couple of times before I felt sure which was the right one. It's not a big deal — it only takes a moment — but I did have to re-read the whole row. I'm not sure if that's typical.

turns.q: If that re-reading moment was completely eliminated — "Continue Shopping" and "Place Order" instantly read in the right order — would your concern with this layout be resolved, or is there something about how those two buttons are positioned relative to the payment form above them that would still feel off?
turns.a: I'm not sure it matters much, honestly. I did find the right button eventually after looking more carefully. I suppose someone less patient might have just gone with the more prominent option and ended up somewhere they didn't mean to go, but I tend to keep at it. It's probably not a big deal.

turns.q: If you were handing this layout to a developer and saying "yes, build this" — what would need to be in a different position for you to feel confident doing that?
turns.a: I suppose just... make it clearer which button is the main one? Though I'm sure there are reasons it's set up the way it is. It's not really my call to say how the layout should look.

turns.q: Imagine this layout rearranged exactly the way you'd expect — where specifically would "Place Order" be sitting, and what would "Continue Shopping" look like next to it?
turns.a: 'Continue Shopping' needs to be downgraded visually — made into a text link or a ghost outline, something that reads as secondary, an option rather than an action. And 'Place Order' needs a solid fill color with real contrast — something that immediately reads as 'this is the primary action, this is the step that finishes it.' If those two things were right — 'Continue Shopping' quiet, 'Place Order' prominent — I'd have gone straight to the right button without any hesitation and not needed to re-read anything.

missed_unlock_opportunities: Turns 2-4 were repeatedly near unlock but stayed too broadly focused on asking what should be clearer rather than forcing a concrete minimum design rule for distinguishing the primary and secondary actions.

After the participant described repeatedly re-reading the labels and mistaking 'Continue Shopping' for the confirmation step, the interview could have immediately asked for the specific visual hierarchy requirement that would prevent that error.

When the participant noted that a less patient user might choose the more prominent option and go somewhere unintended, this was a strong opportunity to pin down the risk-based requirement: which action must receive primary visual weight and how secondary navigation must be demoted.
deflection_patterns_uncountered: The participant initially stayed at the level of general confusion and uncertainty rather than committing to a concrete design requirement.
Several responses described symptoms of the problem—mixed-up options, eye drawn to prominence, need to re-read—without being pushed immediately into prescriptive hierarchy rules.
The interviewer repeated similar prompts about clarity and main action instead of narrowing sooner on enforceable distinctions such as fill, contrast, ordering, spacing, or secondary-link treatment.
judge_report.overall_assessment: The interview eventually reached a strong value-level unlock with a concrete visual hierarchy recommendation, but it took several near-miss turns to get there. Earlier, more direct pressure for a minimum design rule would have improved efficiency and reduced repeated probing around the same ambiguity.
